Senses.Explanation: Literally, to put out the tongue. The Chan record repeatedly makes this visible gesture part of public encounters, but does not give it one invariant emotional gloss. Huangbo involuntarily sticks out his tongue (不覺吐舌, “without realizing it, stuck out his tongue”) on hearing that Baizhang was deaf for three days after Mazu's shout. Elsewhere a visitor sticks out his tongue and says, “truly a dragon-elephant”; a monk leaves with his tongue out after a rebuke; and a later monk says that the teacher's gesture shows he has been caught out. Masters also deliberately use the action as an answer: Nanyuan sticks out his tongue when asked for “one word,” and Zhongqing opens his mouth and sticks out his tongue when asked what his appearance as abbot is for. Thus the ordinary bodily gesture is bent into an answer or demonstrative act in the teaching hall as well as remaining a recorded reaction; the texts themselves decide its local force, and this entry does not assign one motive to every occurrence.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 548 matches in 194 texts. The retained evidence covers involuntary reaction, spoken appraisal, answer to a one-word question, answer concerning an abbot's public function, and an adversarial interview. Formula searches yielded no corpus-wide verbal definition. Family revalidation against “tongue; capacity to speak” (舌頭) and the “broad, long tongue-mark” (廣長舌相) supports one action sense: reaction and deliberate answer are different deployments of the same bodily act, not different things under depth-gate item 8.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老僧昔被馬大師一喝。直得三日耳聾。黃檗聞舉。不覺吐舌。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium (五燈會元), in the Baizhang Huaihai section. Huangbo Xiyun is the exact actor: after Baizhang recounts Mazu's shout and his own three days of deafness, Huangbo hears the account and involuntarily sticks out his tongue (黃檗聞舉，不覺吐舌). Baizhang is the preceding speaker and Mazu the person discussed.
